summary: Revises RIPv2 cryptographic authentication, adding details of using the SHA family of hash algorithms, where RFC 2082 specified only MD5. It obsoletes RFC 2082 and updates RFC 2453.

plainLanguage.summary: This document lets a router prove that a RIP update really came from a neighbour, by putting a keyed fingerprint in the packet instead of a cleartext password. The receiver recomputes the fingerprint and checks a counter that never goes backwards, and drops the packet if either check fails. It also adds the SHA family of hash functions to the older MD5 method.

questions: how does ripv2 key rollover work
subtitle: How RIPv2 routers put a keyed fingerprint in every routing update so a neighbour can check where it came from.

tldr.problem: RIPv2 could send a cleartext password in its updates, so anyone who captured a packet could read the password and inject false routes. The earlier cryptographic version, RFC 2082, offered only the Keyed-MD5 mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: Each update carries an authentication trailer: a Key ID, a data length, a non-decreasing sequence number and the output of a keyed hash function over the packet. The receiver recomputes that output with the key it holds and discards the packet when the two differ.
tldr.outcome: This document keeps Keyed-MD5 for compatibility and adds HMAC with SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. It replaced RFC 2082 and updates RFC 2453, the RIPv2 base specification.

today: RFC 4822 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It replaced RFC 2082, the first version of RIPv2 cryptographic authentication, and updates RFC 2453, the RIPv2 base specification.

sections.title: Why RIPv2 Authentication Was Revised
sections.content:
RIPv2 offers unauthenticated service and password authentication, and this document says both are open to passive attacks, in which someone reads traffic as it passes. The password travels in clear, so anyone who captures one packet can read the password and then inject false routing information into the network.

The earlier RIPv2 cryptographic authentication specification, RFC 2082, used the Keyed-MD5 mechanism. There are no openly published attacks on it, but some reports raise concern about the ultimate strength of the MD5 hash function. Some end users, particularly several different governments, require the SHA hash function family for policy reasons. The older specification also used a hashing construction widely believed to be weaker than the HMAC construction used here.

This document keeps Keyed-MD5, so equipment that already implements RFC 2082 keeps working, and adds HMAC with the SHA family. The mechanism is meant to reduce the risk of a passive attack. It does not hide the routing information, because the purpose of a routing protocol is to publish the topology of the network.
sections.plainLanguage: RIP updates used to carry a plain password, so anyone who could see the packets could read the password and send false routing information. This document replaces the password with a fingerprint computed from a shared secret key, so a fake update cannot be produced without the key. It also adds the SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 options alongside the older MD5 one.

sections.title: The RIPv2 Authentication Trailer
sections.content:
A normal RIPv2 message has an 8-octet header and an array of 20-octet records. When cryptographic authentication is enabled, the header and records stay the same, but the 16-octet password field of the original specification is reused to carry a packet offset to the Authentication Data, a Key Identifier, the Authentication Data Length, and a non-decreasing sequence number.

The Authentication Type is the Cryptographic Hash Function, which is the value 3. The RIPv2 Packet Length is an unsigned 16-bit offset from the start of the RIPv2 header to the end of the regular RIPv2 packet, not counting the authentication trailer. The Key Identifier is an unsigned 8-bit field; together with the network interface it identifies which RIPv2 Security Association is in use for this packet. The Authentication Data Length is an unsigned 8-bit field holding the length in octets of the trailing Authentication Data. It exists so that the mechanism stays independent of the hash function chosen.

The Authentication Data is the output of the keyed hash function. It is not truncated, so its length is the digest size of the hash function in use. The document's packet diagram notes 20 bytes with HMAC-SHA-1, and notes that hash functions with larger output sizes also make the packet longer on the wire.
sections.plainLanguage: The router adds a small block of fields to the end of the normal RIP packet. It names which key was used, says how long the fingerprint is, and carries a counter that only ever goes up. The fingerprint follows, and its length depends on the hash function in use.

sections.title: The RIPv2 Security Association
sections.content:
A RIPv2 Security Association is the set of shared configuration that a legitimate sender and a legitimate receiver both need. It is tied to an interface rather than to a router. The sender picks one based on the outgoing interface; the receiver picks one from the Key Identifier in the packet plus the interface the packet arrived on. If several valid associations exist for the same outgoing interface, the sender may use any of them.

The minimum data items are the Key Identifier, an unsigned 8-bit number; the authentication algorithm, which is never sent over the wire, so the implementer chooses its own representation; the authentication key, which must never be sent over the network in cleartext by any protocol; the sequence number, an unsigned 32-bit number that must not decrease for a given Key ID and sender; a start time, when the association first becomes valid; and a stop time, when it expires. Setting the stop time to never expire is permitted but not recommended, because it is less secure than periodic rekeying.

An implementation must support at least two concurrent associations on each RIP interface. That is what makes key rollover possible.
sections.plainLanguage: A security association is the set of settings two routers share for one interface: the key, the hash function, the key number, and the times the settings are valid. The sending router picks it by outgoing interface, and the receiving router picks it by the key number in the packet.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving an Authenticated Update
sections.content:
When a router creates a packet, it fills in the Authentication Type, chooses a valid security association for the outgoing interface, writes the offset, Key ID and Authentication Data Length, runs the algorithm-specific computation, and writes the result into the Authentication Data field. The UDP checksum should be calculated, but may be set to zero, because the cryptographic mechanism gives stronger integrity protection than the standard UDP checksum.

When a router receives a packet, it sets the received Authentication Data aside, finds the security association from the Key Identifier and the receiving interface, recomputes the Authentication Data, and compares it with what arrived. If they differ, the message must be discarded without being processed and a security event should be logged, recording at least the time, the source IP address, the Key ID, the interface, and the fact that authentication failed. If no valid association exists for that Key ID on that interface, processing also stops and a security event is logged.

The receiver keeps the last sequence number it accepted for each sender and association. If a packet arrives with a lower sequence number than the last one, and the neighbour has been heard from recently enough to have viable routes, the packet must be discarded unprocessed and the event logged. When connectivity to the neighbour has been lost, the receiver should accept either a message with sequence number zero or one with a higher sequence number than the last received.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender computes the fingerprint over the packet, writes it in, and sends. The receiver looks up the matching key by the key number and the interface, recomputes the fingerprint, and drops the packet if the two differ. It also drops a packet whose counter is lower than the last one it accepted from that sender.

sections.title: Keyed-MD5 and HMAC-SHA Processing
sections.content:
With Keyed-MD5, the authentication key is always 16 octets. The key is appended to the packet in memory, the MD5 padding and the 64-bit message length fields are added, and the digest is computed as defined in RFC 1321.

The HMAC processing uses the terminology of FIPS PUB 198. The key is prepared to be exactly L octets long, where L is the length of the hash in octets, so 20 for SHA-1: a key longer than L is replaced by its hash, and a shorter key is padded with zeros. The internal block size B is 64 octets for SHA-1 and SHA-256, and 128 octets for SHA-384 and SHA-512. Opad is the value 0x5c repeated B times, Ipad is 0x36 repeated B times, and Apad is 0x878FE1F3 repeated L/4 times.

The Authentication Data field is first filled with Apad. The inner hash is H(Ko XOR Ipad || packet) and the outer hash is H(Ko XOR Opad || First-Hash). The outer hash becomes the authentication data, and its length is always the digest size of the hash function in use. Because the RIPv2 packet is hashed only once, the cost of hashing twice is negligible. Any key value known to be weak for an algorithm in the NIST Secure Hash Standard must not be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Keyed-MD5 appends the 16-octet key to the packet and hashes the result. The HMAC options hash twice: the first pass mixes the key with the packet, the second pass mixes the key with that first result. The output is not shortened, so a hash with a bigger output makes a longer packet.

sections.title: Key Distribution and Rollover
sections.content:
Each key has its own Key Identifier and its own lifetime, and implementations must be able to store more than one key at the same time. Manual key distribution must be supported, for example an operator typing the key, its lifetime and its identifier on the router console. The document recommends rekeying regularly, with a moderately short association lifetime such as 24 hours, rather than setting the lifetime to infinite. Manual deletion of active associations must also be supported.

The receiver must not simply try every association configured on the receiving interface until one works, because that creates an easily exploited denial-of-service attack against the RIP subsystem. Instead it looks up the association from the Key Identifier and the interface. This makes a smooth rollover possible: each router is updated with the new association several minutes before the current one expires and several minutes before the new lifetime begins, so for a while either key authenticates a message.

An integrated key management protocol is deliberately left out. Such protocols have a history of subtle flaws discovered long after they were published, and embedding one would mean changing every RIPv2 implementation if a flaw turned up. The Key Identifier field is described as a hook for a future standard protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router must hold two keys at once, so a new key can be added before the old one is withdrawn. The router then sends with both keys until every neighbour has moved over. The document does not define a key distribution protocol, so keys are entered by an operator or by a site script.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism is believed to be secure against passive attacks. Protection against active attacks is incomplete. The main gap is a router that has just rebooted and has no non-volatile storage for its associations and last sequence numbers, which leaves a small opening for a replay attack.

Two pathological cases must be handled. During a rollover, a router should detect which associations its neighbours are using and send with both the old and the new one until every neighbour has switched or the old one expires. If the last association on an interface expires, the router must notify the network manager and should treat that association as having an infinite lifetime rather than fall back to unauthenticated routing. Every expiration must be logged, and implementations should offer a fail secure option that lets an operator stop RIPv2 instead of running it insecurely.

Configuring the associations or the authentication type with SNMP is not recommended, even with SNMPv3, because a compromise there would cascade to every router reachable from the compromised one. Using RADIUS or Diameter for the same purpose is also not recommended. Reading the associations with SNMP is allowed, but the information is security-sensitive. The mechanism gives no confidentiality and no protection against traffic analysis, and bulk link encryption is suggested when traffic analysis matters. Implementations should also accept keys in hexadecimal form, because a text-only interface makes many key bits predictable.
sections.plainLanguage: The fingerprint stops someone who cannot read the packets from inventing them, but it does not hide the routing information, and a recorded packet can still be replayed, although the counter limits how long that works. A router that loses its counter after a restart can be tricked for a short time, so the counter should be stored on disk.

viz.caption: THE FIELDS OF THE RIPv2 AUTHENTICATION TRAILER (RFC 4822)

fields.name: Authentication Type
fields.desc: Cryptographic Hash Function, which is the value 3.

fields.name: RIPv2 Packet Length
fields.desc: Offset from the start of the RIPv2 header to the end of the regular packet, not counting the trailer.

fields.name: Key ID
fields.desc: Together with the interface, selects the RIPv2 Security Association for this packet.

fields.name: Auth Data Len
fields.desc: Length in octets of the trailing Authentication Data.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Non-decreasing for all messages from a given source router with a given Key ID.

fields.name: Authentication Data
fields.desc: Output of the keyed hash function. Variable length: 20 bytes with HMAC-SHA-1.

messages.label: UPDATE WITH TRAILER
messages.note: Carries the Key ID, the data length, a sequence number and the authentication data.

messages.label: RECOMPUTE AND COMPARE
messages.note: The receiver looks up the association by Key ID and interface, then recomputes the authentication data.

messages.label: ACCEPT OR DISCARD
messages.note: A mismatch, or a sequence number lower than the last one, means the packet is discarded and logged.
